rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to reveal the full elution window for all 10 compounds while minimizing the risk of truncation. This gives a good first map of early vs late peaks and whether temperature or gradient steepness should be adjusted next.

All 10 compounds eluted well within the broad scout, so trim the gradient window to the actual elution region to reduce time penalty while keeping similar slope and all peaks inside the gradient. This should test whether a narrower, more targeted window can preserve full resolution with a shorter effective separation range.

The scout already had perfect resolution, so the best opportunity is to cut analysis time aggressively while checking whether the critical mid-run cluster still stays above acceptable resolution under a steeper gradient. This slope change will also reveal how sensitive the closest pairs are to gradient steepness.

The 10 min run is very fast but over-compresses the critical 5–7 cluster, while 20 min gives full resolution with only a modest time penalty. An intermediate gradient should recover the failing pair enough to improve the resolution term while keeping the run much shorter than 20 min.

The critical pair improves strongly with shallower slope, and 14 min is already close to optimal, so a small step to 16 min should test whether the 6/7 pair can cross into fully acceptable resolution while keeping zero time penalty. This directly refines around the current best point.

Since the tG optimum at 40 C is already tightly bracketed by 14 and 16 min, the next lever is temperature to see whether the stubborn 6/7 pair reflects selectivity rather than only slope. A modest 5 C decrease should slightly lengthen retention and may improve that pair’s resolution without pushing the run out of the zero-penalty region.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity and shifted the critical overlap to a different pair, so test the opposite direction. A 5 C increase may improve the crowded mid-cluster selectivity while keeping the same near-optimal gradient length and likely preserving zero time penalty.

Temperature clearly changes selectivity within the crowded central cluster, so combine the lower temperature with a steeper gradient to see whether the shifted worst pair can be separated while keeping the run very short. This orthogonal test helps map whether temperature and slope together can outperform the current 14 min, 40 C optimum.

The best region is clearly around 14–16 min at 40 C, and 12 min at 40 C is the missing point needed to define the local CRF maximum versus gradient time. This will show whether the rise from 10 to 14 min is smooth enough that 12 min might beat 14 min by retaining zero time penalty with better-than-expected resolution.

At 40 C the limiting pair responds strongly to slope, and 16 min already achieves full resolution with only a tiny time penalty. Testing 18 min will show whether CRF declines monotonically past 16 min or whether a slightly shallower gradient gains enough resolution margin to offset the extra run time.

Most peaks elute by roughly phi_e 0.25–0.40, so the current 0.95 endpoint is likely broader than needed and may be steeper than optimal through the useful window. Reducing phi1 slightly while holding tG at the current best should shallow the effective gradient enough to improve the critical central pair without adding much total time, while still easily eluting the late peak.

Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the best run, suggesting the useful gradient window is still narrower than the original scout. A further small reduction to 0.85 should test whether the critical 6/7 pair continues to benefit from the shallower slope while likely keeping all compounds inside the gradient and within zero time penalty.

The best result so far came from slightly narrowing the gradient window, while 12 min at phi1 0.95 was a bit too steep. Combining the improved phi1 of 0.90 with a shorter 12 min gradient tests whether that narrower window can recover enough of the critical-pair resolution to beat the current best while keeping a shorter run.

At phi1 0.90 the 14 min run is the best so far, so the next high-value refinement is a slightly shallower slope to see if the 6/7 pair can move from R 1.36 to full resolution while keeping only a very small time penalty. This directly tests whether the local optimum sits just above the current best.

The narrowed window at phi1 0.90 is best, but temperature has only been tested with the broader phi1 0.95 method. Checking 35 C here will show whether selectivity changes become favorable once the gradient window is better focused around the crowded central cluster.

With phi1 0.90, lowering temperature again worsened selectivity and shifted the bottleneck to pair 5/6, so test the opposite direction at the current best gradient window. This checks whether 45 C with the improved phi1 can sharpen the critical cluster better than it did under the broader 0.95 endpoint.

Temperature is clearly not the winning lever, so continue optimizing the gradient window around the best 14 min, 40 C condition. Since narrowing from 0.95 to 0.90 helped and 0.85 still gave full resolution with only a tiny time penalty, testing 0.80 checks whether the resolution gain can outweigh a modest additional delay of the last peak.

The current best is strong enough that the remaining budget can probe for a selectivity surprise, and temperature effects are non-monotonic across the crowded cluster. Testing 50 C at the best phi window and gradient length checks whether a larger temperature shift can reorder or separate the critical pair better than 45 C did.

Since lower temperature shifts the problematic overlap from 6/7 toward 5/6, pair selectivity is changing rather than simply worsening, and a shallower gradient may exploit that. This run tests an orthogonal combination where extra slope relief at 35 C could spread the newly crowded region enough to reveal a better selectivity/time balance than any single-variable change.

The remaining plausible path to beat the best run is a selectivity surprise from combining a shallower gradient with higher temperature, since the 6/7 pair is strongly slope-sensitive and temperature-sensitive. This tests the opposite orthogonal corner from the failed 18 min, 35 C run and could improve the critical cluster while accepting a modest time penalty.

With only a few injections left and the optimum tightly localized, a slightly shallower gradient than 18 min at the best phi window checks whether the resolution term can approach 1.000 strongly enough to reveal the local CRF ceiling in this region. This is a final slope-mapping point around the current best condition.

The best method is well established, so use the remaining budget to test the only major untried window lever near that optimum: raising phi0 slightly while keeping phi1 and tG fixed. This may redistribute gradient time away from the very early well-resolved peaks and subtly alter selectivity within the crowded middle cluster.

Raising phi0 improved the best method, so now test whether a slightly narrower upper endpoint further optimizes the gradient window around the actual elution region. This is the closest unexplored refinement around the current optimum and could nudge the critical 6/7 pair higher without introducing a time penalty.

You already reached the maximum CRF, so use the remaining injection to map the robustness boundary around the optimum by narrowing the upper endpoint one more step. This checks whether the optimum is a plateau extending below phi1 0.85 or whether 0.85 is the lower edge before time penalty grows.

You already have a perfect CRF method, so use the last injection to probe whether a slightly steeper version can also retain full score and define the robustness of the optimum in tG. This tests whether 14 min is the unique optimum or part of a broader plateau at the best phi window.
